title: The Higgs Boson
hook: An invisible field fills all of space, and the harder a particle drags through it, the more mass it has. Finding the ripple that proved it took 50 years and the world's biggest machine.
key_points: The Higgs field fills all of space — it's everywhere, not localized.
Particles gain mass by interacting with the field; more interaction means more mass.
The Higgs boson is a ripple, or excitation, in that field.
Predicted in the 1960s, it was detected at CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012.
content_html: The Higgs boson answers a deceptively basic question: why do particles have mass at all? The idea is that space is permeated by an invisible Higgs field, present everywhere. Particles acquire mass by interacting with this field — the more strongly a particle couples to it, the harder it is to push around, which is exactly what mass means. A photon, which ignores the field entirely, has no mass and flies at light speed.
extra_html: The boson itself is a ripple in that field, the way a wave is a ripple on water. Theorists predicted it in the 1960s, but confirming it meant catching one of these fleeting ripples — a job that required CERN's Large Hadron Collider, the largest machine ever built. In 2012 the collisions finally revealed it, completing the Standard Model's roster and verifying half a century of theory. Wikipedia recounts the prediction, the search, and the 2012 discovery.

flashcards.prompt: How does a particle get its mass, according to the Higgs mechanism?
flashcards.back_html: By interacting with the Higgs field that fills all of space. The more strongly a particle interacts with it, the more mass it has.

choices.text: A ripple, or excitation, in the Higgs field
A type of quark inside the proton

flashcards.explanation_html: The Higgs boson is a disturbance in the underlying Higgs field — detecting it confirmed the field exists.

flashcards.prompt: Where and when was the Higgs boson first detected?

choices.text: At CERN's Large Hadron Collider in 2012

flashcards.explanation_html: Predicted in the 1960s, the Higgs boson was finally observed at the LHC in 2012, decades after the theory.
